proposals.name: Repairs a mis-specified formulation of the problem
proposals.instruction: Score how far the abstract locates a defect in the standard formulation of its problem and supplies a corrected formulation, versus accepting the standard formulation and improving performance inside it. 10 = the abstract names something specific that the prevailing framing gets wrong (a notion that is too coarse, an assumption that is unwarranted, a quantity everyone ignores), introduces the replacement notion explicitly, and the empirical work reads as a consequence of that repair. 5 = a limitation of prior work is named, but the fix is a technique rather than a change of formulation. 0 = the problem is taken exactly as posed by prior work and the whole contribution is a better method or a better number within it.
proposals.rationale: R20 argues set-equivariance is the wrong notion and installs multiset-equivariance; R13 argues standard concentration cannot characterise intrinsic robustness because it ignores labels, and defines label uncertainty; R32 replaces 'distillation works' with a measured quantity (supervision complexity); R01 recasts offline model-based RL as knowing when to trust the model. All four are dense-high / card-low. By contrast R10 and R36 accept the FL and FSCIL formulations untouched and are card-high. A scorecard built from method-quality criteria has no cell for 'the field was asking the wrong question', so it flattens exactly this.

proposals.name: Portable construct versus branded system bundle
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract leaves behind something another researcher could use without adopting this paper's system. 10 = it introduces a definition, quantity, bound, or structural notion that is separable from the implementation and would be citable on its own. 5 = a method with one reusable trick embedded in it. 0 = the only new name is an acronym for a pipeline assembled from existing parts, and nothing survives detaching that acronym.
proposals.rationale: R32 (supervision complexity), R09 (empirical sandwich bounds on the R-D function), R20 (multiset-equivariance) and R13 (label uncertainty) all hand over a portable object and sit dense-high with low card scores. R10 (FedGLCL), R08 (SELF-PARAM) and R14 (PERSONALITYBENCH plus a neuron-editing recipe) are branded bundles and sit card-high with very low dense. A criterion bank that credits 'proposes a novel named method' cannot distinguish these two cases; this criterion does.

proposals.name: Principled derivation versus assembled module list
proposals.instruction: Score whether the method is presented as following from a stated principle or quantity, such that a competent reader could re-derive it, versus being presented as an assembly of parts. 10 = there is an explicit governing idea (an uncertainty decomposition, a variational objective, an optimisation reformulation, a geometric constraint) and each design choice is visibly downstream of it. 5 = one principled core with several unmotivated add-ons. 0 = an enumeration of components (a wider codebook, longer context, a better discriminator, an extra loss) each justified only by the assertion that it improves results.
proposals.rationale: R01 derives its estimator from epistemic uncertainty and a lower bound on the Bayesian posterior value; R53, R15 and R43 each state the object being optimised before saying what they do; all are dense-high / card-low. R16 lists a broader VQ space, extended context windows, improved attention, a multi-scale discriminator and an inverse Fourier structure with no unifying principle, and R50 stacks attention-guided plus non-local distillation; both are card-high / dense-low. Scorecards reward the presence of many described components; the dense signal appears to reward derivability.

proposals.name: Diagnosis paired with the intervention it predicts
proposals.instruction: Score the coupling between explanation and action. 10 = the abstract states a causal hypothesis about why something fails, derives a concrete intervention from that hypothesis, and reports the intervention's effect in a way that functions as a test of the hypothesis. 5 = a mechanism is proposed but the fix does not obviously follow from it, or a fix is given with a post-hoc story. 0 = a phenomenon or trade-off is measured and the abstract ends with a call for future work rather than an intervention.
proposals.rationale: R23 posits a two-domain hypothesis for clean and adversarial images, then predicts and confirms that removing clean images and splitting the BN statistics buys robustness; R46 walks a diffusion model backwards component by component so each removal is an experiment on the hypothesis. Both are dense-high / card-low. R42 measures a real trade-off and closes with a recommendation to the community, and R26 quantifies a limit and gestures at mitigations; both are card-high / dense-low. A bank crediting 'provides analysis' credits all four equally.

proposals.name: States a limit, bound, or guarantee on what is achievable
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract makes a claim about the boundary of the possible, with its regime stated. 10 = an explicit upper or lower bound, near-optimality, provable separation or margin, existence claim, or complexity result, together with the conditions under which it holds. 5 = a theoretical framework or convergence claim asserted without the regime being visible. 0 = the abstract makes only empirical claims about how one system performed.
proposals.rationale: R09 sandwiches the rate-distortion function and converts the bound into a statement about how much room existing compressors have left; R15 gives an O(m + poly(k/eps)) coreset and argues the dependence on m is nearly optimal; R53 characterises benign, tempered and catastrophic overfitting; R05 guarantees a distinguishable margin; R43 frames model utilisation as an optimisation problem with near-optimal solutions. All are dense-high with card scores between 0.006 and 0.34. A scorecard with a generic 'theoretical grounding' criterion cannot tell a bound on the achievable from a convergence proof attached to a specific algorithm (R40).

proposals.name: One load-bearing thesis versus enumerated thin deliverables
proposals.instruction: Score claim unity against claim count. 10 = a single claim carries the paper, and everything else in the abstract is evidence for that one claim; the reader can restate the paper in one sentence without losing it. 5 = two or three genuinely coupled contributions. 0 = a first/second/third enumeration of loosely related deliverables (a dataset, a model, a pipeline, a finding) where each item gets one clause of support and the items would not miss each other if separated.
proposals.rationale: R11 is three sentences with exactly one thesis and no decoration (dense 0.999, card 0.006); R25, R46 and R49 are likewise single-claim. R14 advertises 'three major technical contributions', R04 runs firstly/then/finally through collection, annotation, reward model, benchmark and fine-tuning, and R16 numbers its advantages; all three are card-high and dense-low. An additive scorecard scores an enumerated abstract once per item and so rewards padding; a reader tracking one idea does not.

proposals.name: Novel object versus novelty by conjunction of qualifiers
proposals.instruction: Score where the novelty lives. 10 = the new thing is new as an object, and the claim would remain interesting if the setting were described in fewer words. 0 = novelty is asserted as 'the first method for A, in the B setting, under C assumptions, with D constraints', where the priority claim survives only because of the conjunction of qualifiers, each of which narrows the population of prior work. Intermediate scores for one or two qualifiers that are themselves substantive.
proposals.rationale: R40 claims 'the very first algorithm to solve FL problems with heterogeneous data in the nonconvex and relaxed smoothness setting' — three stacked qualifiers — and is card 0.849 / dense 0.161; R36 and R10 are similar conjunction claims inside FSCIL and non-IID FL. R20 and R09 introduce objects (multiset-equivariance, an empirical sandwich bound) whose interest does not depend on qualifier stacking, and are dense-high / card-low. Bank criteria of the form 'is the contribution novel' read the priority sentence and cannot discount the qualifiers.

proposals.name: Transplant plus benchmark gain sold as the contribution
proposals.instruction: Score how much the work rests on importing an established technique into a new application area. 10 = no such import, or the import is present but the abstract names the specific obstacle that made it non-trivial and says what had to change for it to work at all. 5 = an import with a plausible but generic difficulty story. 0 = the recipe is visibly 'technique T from area A, applied to problem B, yields benchmark gains', with the act of transfer presented as the contribution and the gains carrying the argument.
proposals.rationale: R10 imports language-driven representation learning into federated learning, R36 imports neural collapse into few-shot class-incremental learning, R34 imports projective clustering into embedding compression; all three are card-high (0.78 to 0.96) and dense-low (0.06 to 0.08). R06 is the instructive middle case: it is also a transplant (dynamic NeRF into physical attacks) but does name the blocking obstacle (texture embedded in network parameters, solved by editing UV maps), and its dense percentile is the lowest of the set even so. A scorecard rewards the novelty-of-application and the reported delta; the transplant pattern is invisible to it.

proposals.name: Durability and generality of the object studied
proposals.instruction: Score how general and long-lived the thing being studied is, independent of how well the study is executed. 10 = the object will still exist and matter regardless of which systems are fashionable — gradient descent dynamics, the final linear layer of a classifier, ridge regression, clustering with outliers, the diffusion-model family as such. 5 = a widely used technique or model family with a clear shelf life. 0 = a single specific architecture or product of narrow and transient interest, where a finding about it does not transfer once that artefact is superseded.
proposals.rationale: R25 (the last weight layer of any classifier), R49 (edge-of-stability dynamics of gradient descent), R53 (kernel ridge regression) and R46 (denoising diffusion models as a family) are all dense-high with card scores from 0.05 to 0.31. R52 does everything right procedurally — three diagnosed defects, three fixes, a 43% error reduction — but the object is one legacy memory architecture, and it lands card 0.985 / dense 0.072; R30 studies user-interest units inside a specific VAE recommender. Execution-quality criteria score R52 highly; a reader weighing what the finding will still buy in five years does not.

proposals.name: Contribution by subtraction rather than addition
proposals.instruction: Score whether the result removes machinery. 10 = the paper shows a standard component is unnecessary, replaces learning with precomputation, freezes what was trained, or reduces a modern method to a classical one, and quantifies what that removal costs. 5 = a simplification of one sub-part alongside additions elsewhere. 0 = the contribution is strictly additive: new modules, new losses, new stages, new supervision.
proposals.rationale: R25 fixes the classifier and asks what is lost; R46 deconstructs a diffusion model until it is nearly a denoising autoencoder; R55 removes training from the message-passing module entirely and precomputes it; R43 removes the ad-hoc use of the learned model in favour of an optimised one. All are dense-high with card 0.05 to 0.17. The additive papers R16 and R50 sit card-high and dense-low. Bank criteria phrased as 'proposes novel components' or 'technical depth' penalise subtraction, which is why the scorecard buries these.

proposals.name: Calibrated, non-uniform reporting of where gains occur
proposals.instruction: Score the calibration of the performance rhetoric against what is actually claimed. 10 = the abstract distinguishes where the method wins, where it merely ties, and where it does not help ('on par or better', 'in most cases', 'competitive', 'state of the art on 11 of 18'), and still commits to a clear claim. 5 = uniformly positive but specific and bounded to named settings. 0 = blanket superiority across every comparison, superlatives without exception, or claims of surpassing whole classes of systems by a substantial margin with no tie or failure acknowledged.
proposals.rationale: R20 reports better results 'in most cases', R44 finds algorithms 'on par or better' than human-designed ones, R37 'performs competitively', R01 is explicit that it is state of the art on 11 of 18 datasets and on par on the rest — all dense-high, card 0.14 to 0.29. R27 surpasses 'all other open-source LLMs by a substantial margin' and R10 'significantly outperforms state-of-the-art FL algorithms across different non-IID scenarios'; both are card-high and dense-low. A judge scoring 'strength of empirical results' from the abstract reads confidence as strength; the honest partial win reads as weakness to the scorecard and as credibility to a reader.

proposals.name: Judged by a domain-meaningful quantity, not only a leaderboard
proposals.instruction: Score whether success is defined by something that would still matter to a practitioner in the application domain if the benchmark disappeared. 10 = the abstract commits to a criterion with external meaning — physical or energetic plausibility, chemical validity of substructures, expert paleographic or clinical annotation, behaviour under missing sensors, compatibility with an established domain method — and reports against it. 5 = benchmark metrics plus one domain-flavoured metric. 0 = every reported quantity is a score on a shared benchmark and no external notion of correctness appears.
proposals.rationale: R31 reports the fraction of energetically favourable poses rising from 30% to 73%, not only docking accuracy; R19 insists on valid, realistic substructures alongside affinity, QED and SA; R24 is judged by whether it integrates with fast multipole methods and QM/MM; R07 tests leave-sensor-out on healthcare series. All are dense-high with card 0.06 to 0.31. Card-high items such as R47 and R21 report FID, preference rates and qualitative applications only. A scorecard criterion for 'rigorous evaluation' counts metrics; it does not ask whether any of them mean something outside the leaderboard.

proposals.name: Evaluation designed to break the claim, not to cover ground
proposals.instruction: Score whether at least one evaluation was chosen because it could have falsified the central claim. 10 = the abstract names a stress setting selected for difficulty — a held-out structural factor, the strictest available metric, black-box or unseen-condition transfer, an ablation that could show a component is worthless — and reports the outcome there. 5 = standard benchmarks plus routine ablations. 0 = breadth only: many datasets, many models, many modalities, all reported favourably, with no setting where the claim was at risk.
proposals.rationale: R07 reports the challenging leave-sensor-out setting; R20 reports 8% to 77% under 'one of the strictest evaluation metrics'; R05 pairs OOD detection gains with an explicit check that in-distribution accuracy is not sacrificed. All are dense-high / card-low. R12 evaluates 22 open-source and 6 closed models across five modalities and R41 spans three architectures and many benchmarks — impressive coverage, no risk — and both are card-high with dense at 0.31 and 0.07. Coverage is easy to score from an abstract and is what a criterion bank will pick up; risk is not.

proposals.name: Substantive claim versus adoption-contingent resource provision
proposals.instruction: Score what the paper would be worth if nobody used its artefacts. 10 = the central contribution is a proposition or a method whose correctness stands on its own; the reader learns something true whether or not any resource is downloaded. 5 = a claim supported by a new resource built for the purpose. 0 = the contribution is the resource itself — a benchmark, dataset, metric, probe, tokenizer or pipeline — with the substantive assertions being that it exists, that it is comprehensive, and that current systems score variably on it.
proposals.rationale: R12 (LOKI: 18K questions, 26 subcategories), R04 (ProactiveBench: 6,790 events plus a reward model), R14 (PERSONALITYBENCH), R35 (ImpScore) and R33 (a benchmark task plus dataset for picture-word interference) are all card-high (0.83 to 0.99) and dense-low (0.00 to 0.31). Resource abstracts are unusually easy to score well on an explicit bank: they state scale, curation, coverage, evaluation breadth and availability in plain language, hitting many criteria at once, while the residual claim is thin.

proposals.name: Unfashionable bet stated plainly, without hedging apparatus
proposals.instruction: Score intellectual risk. 10 = the paper commits to a direction that could plainly have failed and is not the safe move of the moment — a new algebraic structure inside attention, searching over programs instead of over weights, running a modern model backwards toward a classical one, building a toy object to explain a real phenomenon — and states it without surrounding itself with the customary reassurances. 5 = a mainstream direction pursued with one genuinely non-obvious choice. 0 = squarely inside the currently popular recipe, hedged by including every expected ingredient (scale, ablations, artefacts, breadth) so that the work cannot be wrong about anything in particular.
proposals.rationale: R11 proposes higher-dimensional attention with tensor products for logical reasoning in three sentences with no numbers, no baselines and no artefacts (dense 0.999, card 0.006 — the widest gap in the slice); R44 meta-learns curiosity as programs rather than transferring weights; R46 argues for walking back to a classical denoising autoencoder; R49 deliberately builds a minimalist function rather than another large-scale study. All are dense-high. R41 and R08 take safe, well-populated directions and pad them out, and are card-high. A criterion bank rewards the presence of expected ingredients, so the plainly stated bet with none of them scores near zero on almost every cell.

proposals.name: Sheer abstract length and clause verbosity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much prose is present and how elaborated it is, independent of what it says. Count words, sentences, paragraph breaks, and the amount of subordinate elaboration per sentence. Anchors: 0 = extremely short (roughly three sentences or fewer, one compact block, no elaboration); 3 = one short paragraph; 5 = one full paragraph of ordinary length; 8 = long, multi-paragraph, with several elaborated or enumerated details; 10 = very long and densely elaborated across multiple paragraphs. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the prose is clear or well written, or whether the underlying work is good. Volume only.
proposals.rationale: A fixed criterion bank can only fire on criteria whose evidence is textually present, so word count mechanically buys coverage: an item that never mentions datasets, ablations or availability cannot score on those criteria however strong the work is. In this slice the shortest items sit on the dense_high_card_low side (R06 is three sentences; R42, R27, R11, R43 and R25 are all single short blocks), while the long, elaborated items sit on the dense_low_card_high side (R24, R46, R59, R39, R53). Length is not research quality: R06 and R42 are compact statements of a construction, not thin work.

proposals.name: Canonical abstract-template completeness and explicit signposting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how completely the text executes the standard machine-learning conference abstract template and how explicitly it signposts the moves. The moves are: (1) a broad context sentence; (2) an explicit gap or limitation of prior work, usually opened by 'However'; (3) an 'In this paper we propose <NAMED SYSTEM>' sentence; (4) an itemised walk through components or steps; (5) an explicit statement that experiments were run; (6) a closing significance or availability sentence. Add credit for visible signposting devices: 'First,/Second,/Third,', '1) ... 2) ...', bullets, bold or italic emphasis on key terms, one-claim-per-line layout. Anchors: 0 = few moves present and no signposting; 5 = most moves present but run together as continuous prose; 10 = every move present, in order, with explicit enumeration or emphasis markup. Score only the presence, ordering and explicitness of the structure. You must NOT judge whether the structure is used well, whether the claims inside it are true, or whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Template compliance is a fingerprint of an unseen factor - how drilled the writer is in this genre - and a criterion-bank scorer is a checklist, so a fully executed checklist scores well by construction. R33 spells out 'three major technical contributions. First... Second... Third...', R24 numbers its advantages '1) extreme compression... 2) improved subjective quality', R10 bolds its two named desiderata and R35 numbers its two diagnosed causes; all four are dense_low_card_high. R06, R12, R27 and R43 skip most moves and are dense_high_card_low. Tagged mixed because practised writers may also do genuinely better work.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's training and practice in the conference-submission format (advisor and lab boilerplate, number of prior submissions)

proposals.name: Artifact-availability boilerplate and repository links
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit availability statements for code, data, models or a project page. Look for URLs (github.com, project pages), and for phrases such as 'the code is available at', 'publicly available', 'codes have been released', 'our data and code can be found at', 'model weights and data are public'. Anchors: 0 = no mention of any artifact being available; 3 = a bare unlinked mention such as 'code will be released'; 6 = one explicit link or one clear availability sentence; 10 = a prominent availability sentence naming several artifact types (code, data, checkpoints, benchmark) with URLs. Do not visit or evaluate any link, and do not judge whether releasing artifacts is good practice or whether the work is good. Presence and prominence of the boilerplate only.
proposals.rationale: Release practice is set by lab norms and engineering headcount, not by the merit of the idea, but it leaves a crisp textual trace that a criterion bank almost certainly has a criterion for ('are artifacts available?'). In this slice, availability boilerplate clusters hard on the dense_low_card_high side: R32, R36, R51, R59, R16, R05, R34, R29, R39. Items with no availability sentence at all cluster on the dense_high_card_low side: R06, R11, R27, R42, R22, R44. Tagged mixed because well-resourced labs that release code may also produce better work; R37 shows the trace is not deterministic.
proposals.upstream_parent: the producing lab's engineering resources and open-source release practice

proposals.name: Density of quantified head-to-head improvement numerals
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how densely the text carries explicit numeric performance figures attached to comparisons. Count percentages, absolute metric points, multiplicative speedups, named metric abbreviations tied to numbers (AUROC, AP, F1, FID, PSNR, dB), and before/after phrasings such as 'from 30% to 73%' or 'reduces error by 43%'. Anchors: 0 = no performance numerals anywhere; 3 = a single vague number; 6 = two or three numeric comparisons; 10 = many precise numeric deltas, several tied to named baselines or named metrics. Score only presence and density of such numerals. You must NOT judge whether the numbers are large, correct, fairly obtained or impressive, and not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Whether an abstract can display numeric deltas is largely decided by subfield convention, not by how much was learned: a coreset bound or a deconstruction study has nothing of this shape to report. A criterion bank that asks 'are improvements quantified against baselines?' converts that convention into score. Number-dense items here are dense_low_card_high: R03 (92.7% versus 28.5%), R35 (43.9 AP, 4.1 higher), R45 (43%), R58 (66.47% F1), R08 (40% compression, 0.5% versus 2.8% drop), R59 (3.25x, 4.5x). Number-free items are dense_high_card_low: R06, R12, R25, R27, R42, R43. Tagged mixed because a subfield's measurement culture can also drive real rigour, and R01, R07, R48 and R56 carry numerals on the other side of the slice.
proposals.upstream_parent: reporting conventions of the author's subfield (empirical benchmark culture versus theoretical or conceptual culture)

proposals.name: Compute-scale and infrastructure resource signalling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of textual signals of large computational or infrastructural resources. Look for: parameter counts in the billions; named hardware (TPU pods, A100, A6000, multi-GPU); GPU-hours or wall-clock training times; very large batch sizes; web-scale or ImageNet-scale corpora; training, fine-tuning or evaluating many models or many baselines; unusually deep or wide networks presented as reachable. Anchors: 0 = no resource signal at all; 3 = one incidental mention (a standard dataset name only); 6 = one clear scale boast; 10 = several explicit scale signals (hardware plus counts plus timing). Score only how loudly resources are signalled in the text. You must NOT judge whether the compute was well spent, whether scale is scientifically warranted, or whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Compute budget is an unseen property of who produced the item, but it leaves an unmistakable trace, and a criterion bank asking about 'scale and thoroughness of evaluation' reads that trace as merit. R41 advertises batch size 32868, a TPUv3 Pod and 76 minutes; R59 advertises 175 billion parameters, four GPU hours, A100 and A6000; R46 advertises 22 open-source plus 6 closed models over 18K questions; all three are dense_low_card_high. Resource-silent items such as R11, R15, R26 and R42 are dense_high_card_low. Tagged mixed because compute access plausibly also enables genuinely stronger evidence.
proposals.upstream_parent: the producing group's compute budget and industrial or well-funded-lab affiliation

proposals.name: Named-benchmark or dataset construction framed as headline contribution
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which building a named benchmark, dataset or annotation resource is presented as a headline contribution, together with counted scale. Look for a capitalised or branded resource name introduced with 'we construct', 'we introduce', 'we collect'; explicit counts of items, categories, difficulty levels, annotators or evaluated systems; description of a human-annotation or curation pipeline. Anchors: 0 = no dataset or benchmark contribution mentioned; 3 = an existing public dataset merely used; 6 = a modest new evaluation set mentioned in passing; 10 = a named resource presented as the central contribution with explicit counts and a described curation or annotation process. Score only how prominently resource-construction is foregrounded and quantified. You must NOT judge whether the resource is needed, well designed, or whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Resource-building is bought with money and headcount rather than insight, and it is unusually legible to a criterion bank (it satisfies contribution, novelty, evaluation-breadth and reproducibility criteria at once). In this slice R33 (PERSONALITYBENCH), R46 (LOKI: 18K questions, 26 subcategories, 22 plus 6 models) and R58 (ProactiveBench: 6,790 events, human annotators, learned reward model) are all dense_low_card_high and sit at the very top of the card side; R36 and R05 add curated pairs plus expert annotations on the same side. Nothing on the dense_high_card_low side foregrounds a constructed resource. Tagged mixed because annotation budget can also buy genuinely better evidence.
proposals.upstream_parent: annotation budget, team size and access to human labellers or expert annotators

proposals.name: Theory-subcommunity register: in-abstract citations, notation, guarantees
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the text is written in the register of a theory or algorithms subcommunity. Components: (a) literature citations placed inside the abstract itself, with author names and years and sometimes venue tags such as SODA, FOCS or 'cf. Author et al. 2022'; (b) inline mathematical notation and typeset math (set symbols, epsilon, k-Median, big-O or poly expressions, subscripted variables); (c) claims stated as bounds, optimality, near-optimality or rigorous proof rather than as a table of benchmark wins. Anchors: 0 = none of these; 4 = notation but no citations and no formal guarantee; 7 = two components clearly present; 10 = in-abstract citations plus heavy notation plus explicit guarantee or proof claims. Score register only. You must NOT judge whether the theory is deep, correct, or interesting, and you must NOT reward or penalise the absence of experiments.
proposals.rationale: Which community trained the writer is invisible, but its house style is not, and a criterion bank written around empirical-paper virtues systematically misreads that style as missing content. R02 cites [Feldman and Schulman, SODA'12], [Huang et al., FOCS'18] and [Braverman et al., FOCS'22] inline and states a size bound; R11 carries an agnostic-risk framing with 'cf. Mallinar et al. 2022'; R37 cites Gibson 2017, Blahut 1972, Arimoto 1972 and Balle et al. inside the abstract. All three are dense_high_card_low with low card side. Tagged mixed because subcommunity training also shapes real rigour, so the parent is not purely a nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's home subcommunity and the abstract-writing conventions it trains into its members

proposals.name: Promotional intensifier and significance-boilerplate density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the density of promotional wording and closing significance boilerplate, independent of whether it is deserved. Count occurrences of: 'state-of-the-art', 'significantly outperforms', 'by a large margin', 'extensive experiments', 'comprehensive', 'novel', 'remarkably', 'notably', 'extraordinary', 'striking', 'superior', 'crucial', 'paves the way for', 'highlights the potential of', 'opens the door to'. Anchors: 0 = plain descriptive prose with no intensifiers; 3 = one or two; 6 = several, including one significance closer; 10 = intensifiers throughout plus an explicit future-significance closing sentence. Score how promotional the surface wording is. You must NOT judge whether the enthusiasm is warranted, whether the claims are true, or whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Intensifier density is essentially free to produce and is decided at the polishing stage rather than by what was found, yet a judge scoring criteria like 'clarity of contribution' or 'demonstrated impact' will be moved by it. R18 stacks 'remarkable', 'extraordinary capabilities', 'Remarkably', 'surpasses all other open-source LLMs by a substantial margin'; R28 closes 'significantly outperforms state-of-the-art'; R33 has 'Extensive experiments validates... Notably'; R10 and R58 both close with a 'paves the way' sentence; all are dense_low_card_high. R12 closes with the anti-promotional 'We hope our study will rekindle interest', R26 and R25 stay flatly descriptive, and these are dense_high_card_low.
proposals.upstream_parent: the writer's promotional habit and the amount of polishing or writing assistance applied before submission

proposals.name: Era-marked vocabulary and frontier-system name-dropping
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the text is date-stamped by the vocabulary and named systems it invokes. Look for: names of contemporaneous flagship systems (GPT-4, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Mistral, Llama-2, YOLOv8, BERT, CLIP, NeRF); moment-marking openers such as 'With the rapid development of AI-generated content', 'Recent advances in large language models', 'the future internet may be inundated with'; and currently fashionable object nouns (LLM agents, multimodal, diffusion, codec tokenizer, model merging). Anchors: 0 = the topic vocabulary carries no date stamp and would read the same in any year; 4 = one dated term late in the text; 7 = a dated opener or one flagship system named early; 10 = several dated names or phrases within the first two sentences. Score datedness and fashion-marking only. You must NOT judge whether the topic is important, timely in a good way, or whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: The cycle an item was written in is invisible but leaves a heavy lexical trace, and criteria phrased around 'timeliness', 'relevance' or 'importance of the problem' convert fashion into score. Every heavily era-marked item in this slice is dense_low_card_high: R18 (GPT-4, ChatGPT-3.5, Claude Instant, Gemini Pro, Mistral Medium), R46 ('rapid development of AI-generated content'), R58 (LLM agents), R10, R34, R50, R33. The dense_high_card_low side is dominated by year-agnostic vocabulary: R11, R15, R21, R27, R42, R55. The cycle does not cause the research to be better or worse.
proposals.upstream_parent: which submission cycle the item was written into, and the topical fashion of that cycle

proposals.name: Obvious-first-pairing framing versus late crowded-field riff
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the text reads as one of the first, most obvious readings of its area rather than a late arrival into a worked-over one. High end: the core move is 'technique X has recently shown striking progress; in this paper we bring X to task or domain Y', with X described by the text itself as recent, powerful or popular, and Y a target it has not been pointed at before; the framing assumes the pairing is open ground. Low end: the item reads as arriving into an already-crowded line - it names several specific competing systems, patches a narrow, already-diagnosed failure mode of an established method, deconstructs or minimally re-examines something the community has already built, or assumes the reader knows the obvious approaches are taken. Anchors: 0 = clearly a late, narrow, differentiated increment inside a crowded line; 5 = neither reading dominates; 10 = clearly the obvious first pairing of a currently hot technique with a fresh target. You cannot see when the item was actually written or submitted and must not try to infer a date; score only the rhetorical positioning visible in the text, and you must NOT judge whether being early or late is good, nor whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 channel. Where an item falls in the run of entries on a topic is unobservable, but it dictates the rhetoric available: the first entrants can write the clean 'X meets Y' opening, latecomers must differentiate against named incumbents. A criterion bank rewards the clean opening (clear motivation, clear novelty statement) and reads differentiation as incrementality. Obvious-pairing items here are dense_low_card_high: R03 ('recent research has shown significant progress in using NeRF' then NeRF for person-detector attacks), R28 (language-driven representation learning brought to federated learning), R13 (hypernetworks for the Pareto front), R29 (transformer for colorization). Late-riff items are dense_high_card_low: R12 deconstructs an already-built family, R15 builds a minimalist example of an already-observed phenomenon, R27 revisits the last layer, R55 sharpens an existing DSPN. Tagged mixed because arriving early on a genuinely open pairing can itself be real contribution.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream for this topic - how early the item arrived relative to how crowded its subarea already was

proposals.name: Explains the underlying mechanism, not just the effect
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how explicitly the abstract explains WHY the method or phenomenon works, versus merely reporting THAT it works. A 10: the abstract states an explicit causal/mechanistic account (e.g., a named mechanism, an interplay of factors, a hypothesis about cause) that is argued or shown to connect the intervention to the outcome. A 0: the abstract only states what was built/done and that it improved a number, with zero explanation of why the improvement occurs.
proposals.rationale: R08 (Supervision Complexity) builds a theoretical mechanism (alignment between teacher supervision and student NTK) that explains why distillation tricks work; R41 (CBOP) explains its gain via an explicit epistemic-uncertainty tradeoff mechanism. Both are dense_high_card_low. Contrast with R01, which reports an AP gain with two named techniques but no mechanism for why distillation specifically fails on detection beyond restating the problem.

proposals.name: Names the precise mechanism behind a prior failure
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how precisely the abstract diagnoses a specific, mechanism-level reason existing approaches fail, rather than a vague claim that they are 'limited' or 'suboptimal.' A 10: the abstract names an exact causal chain of failure (e.g., 'navigating to a bad location where the manipulation skill cannot reach its target'). A 0: the abstract asserts prior work is worse/limited with no stated mechanism of failure.
proposals.rationale: R13 (Multi-skill Mobile Manipulation) pinpoints the exact compounding-error mechanism in skill chaining; R59 (Multiset-Equivariant Set Prediction) formally identifies that set-equivariant functions provably cannot represent certain multiset functions. Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R20 or R55, which assert limitation without mechanism and are dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Single unifying idea vs. many bolted-on components
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the method is driven by one small, generalizable mechanism versus a stack of many separately-named modules/tricks. A 10: one core idea does essentially all the work, described in a sentence or two. A 0: the abstract enumerates many distinct named components/modules (three or more) that must work in conjunction, each requiring separate justification.
proposals.rationale: R02 (Fix your classifier) and R53 (2-Simplicial Transformer) are each carried by a single crisp mechanism. Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R07 (WavTokenizer), which stacks a broader VQ space, extended context windows, improved attention, a multi-scale discriminator, and an inverse Fourier transform structure, and is dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Contains a formal proof, bound, or guarantee
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the presence of a stated formal/analytical guarantee (a proof, a bound, a provable property, a rigorous derivation) as opposed to purely empirical claims. A 10: abstract states a specific proven bound or rigorously derived guarantee. A 0: no formal claim of any kind, purely empirical description of experiments and results.
proposals.rationale: R27 (Near-optimal Coresets) states a specific size bound O(m + poly(k, eps^-1)) constructed in near-linear time, proven near-optimal; R51 (Cost of Overfitting in KRR) gives a rigorous characterization of overfitting regimes. Both dense_high_card_low, both purely theoretical with no empirical benchmark bragging.

proposals.name: Proposes a new method/theory vs. diagnostic-only study
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's primary contribution is a new constructive method, algorithm, or theory (10) versus a purely diagnostic/evaluative study that tests, critiques, or characterizes existing systems without proposing a new solution (0).
proposals.rationale: R22 (Can Neural Networks Learn Implicit Logic?), R30 (Steerability of GANs), R36 (Language-biased image classification), and R39 (Is Factuality Enhancement a Free Lunch?) are all diagnostic/evaluative studies of existing models, and all four are dense_low_card_high -- a striking, repeated pattern suggesting the scorecard rewards careful diagnostic rigor that the dense model discounts relative to constructive contributions.

proposals.name: Uses a minimal toy case to explain real phenomena
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract deliberately constructs a simplified/minimal example or reduced model specifically to isolate and explain a phenomenon that is known to occur in complex, real systems. A 10: abstract explicitly builds a toy/minimal construction and shows it reproduces and explains a real-system behavior. A 0: no such reductive move; complexity is not stripped down anywhere.
proposals.rationale: R14 (Understanding Edge-of-Stability with a Minimalist Example) explicitly constructs a simple function reproducing EoS dynamics and bifurcation behavior 'also observed in the training of neural nets'; R50 (Deconstructing Denoising Diffusion Models) explicitly narrates 'deconstructing a DDM... into a classical Denoising Autoencoder' to isolate which components matter. Both dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Conceptual insight independent of released code/data assets
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's persuasive weight rests on a clearly stated, distinct conceptual or methodological insight (10), versus resting mainly on the breadth of released assets (code, data, weights) and exhaustive validation with little distinct insight articulated (0).
proposals.rationale: R45 (Gaussian Ensemble Belief Propagation) combines two existing named methods (EnKF, GaBP) and closes by pointing to supporting code, with the abstract's persuasive weight on applicability across problem types rather than a sharply new idea; R28 (Knowledge Fusion of LLMs) similarly closes on 'code, model weights, and data are public.' Both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Core contribution is a method/theory, not a new benchmark
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's central claimed contribution is a new algorithm, model, or theoretical result (10) versus the construction of a new evaluation resource (benchmark/dataset) accompanied mainly by evaluation of existing models on it (0).
proposals.rationale: R56 (LOKI: a synthetic-data-detection benchmark evaluating 22 open- and 6 closed-source LMMs) and R32 (PERSONALITYBENCH, a large-scale benchmark construction) both center on new-resource construction rather than a new algorithmic idea, and both are dense_low_card_high (dense_pct .313 and .188 respectively, card_pct .991 and .992).

proposals.name: Synthesizes broad evaluation into one clear takeaway
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether, when the abstract invokes multiple datasets/models/metrics, it distills them into one clear, generalizable takeaway (10), versus simply enumerating coverage (many datasets, many baselines, many metrics) without stating what was learned across them (0).
proposals.rationale: R06 (Neural Collapse for FSCIL) validates on three datasets (miniImageNet, CUB-200, CIFAR-100) and closes only with 'outperforms state-of-the-art performances,' without a synthesized insight about why; R56 (LOKI) evaluates 28 models across 5 modalities and 26 subcategories with only a generic closing about 'potential... and limitations.' Both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: One or two numbers anchor the central claim
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's quantitative evidence is concentrated in one or two sharply-stated numbers directly tied to the paper's central claim (10), versus scattered across many loosely-connected statistics that dilute any single headline result (0).
proposals.rationale: R59 (Multiset-Equivariant Set Prediction) anchors its entire claim on one dramatic number: improvement from 8% to 77% on the strictest CLEVR metric; R41 (CBOP) anchors on a small, tightly-scoped comparison table (116.4%, 23.2%, 23.7% gains over three named baselines, 11/18 benchmark wins). Both dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Avoids itemized 'First/Second/Third' contribution-listing structure
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract presents its contributions as an integrated narrative/argument (10) versus as an explicit itemized checklist (e.g., 'First,... Second,... Third,...' or bulleted enumeration of separate results/contributions) (0).
proposals.rationale: R32 (Neuron based Personality Trait Induction) is structured explicitly as 'First,... Second,... Third,...'; R35 (Exponential Learning Rate Schedule) is structured as a bulleted list of three separate new results. Both dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard may reward the appearance of itemized thoroughness that the dense model does not credit as such.

proposals.name: Substantiates comparative claims with explanation, not just naming
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 jointly on two things together: (a) whether the abstract names specific competing systems/methods it claims to beat, and (b) whether it explains the mechanism behind that win. A 10: names competitors AND gives a substantive causal explanation for the win. A 0: names specific competing systems beaten (e.g., other well-known named models) but gives no explanation of the mechanism behind the win, relying on the comparison itself as evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: R10 (WizardMath) claims to outperform 'ChatGPT-3.5, Claude Instant, Gemini Pro and Mistral Medium' with only a passing, unspecific nod to 'instruction evolution and process supervision'; R52 (Proactive Agent) claims to outperform 'all open-source and close-source models' via one F1 number with no mechanism given for the win. Both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: States a broadly general principle vs. narrow one-off fix
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract frames its contribution as a general principle or framework intended to apply across a class of problems/domains (10), versus a fix engineered and validated only within one narrow, specific setting (0).
proposals.rationale: R31 (Understanding Intrinsic Robustness) builds a general label-uncertainty-adjusted concentration estimation framework applicable to any classification problem; R33 (Empirical Sandwich Bounds on R-D Function) explicitly targets 'a general (not necessarily discrete) source requiring only i.i.d. data samples,' generalizing beyond prior distributional assumptions. Both dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Concise, information-dense prose with no throat-clearing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 jointly on abstract length and information density together: whether the abstract is short and nearly every sentence advances a new technical claim (10), versus long with repeated motivation, restated problem framing, or padding sentences that add no new information (0).
proposals.rationale: R02 (Fix your classifier) and R04 (Partitioned Learned Bloom Filters) are both under roughly 120 words, with essentially every sentence carrying new technical content and no restated motivation. Both dense_high_card_low, illustrating that dense scoring does not penalize brevity the way a criterion bank tallying many separately-scored properties might.

proposals.name: Explicitly frames and explains a surprising/counterintuitive finding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explicitly flags a result as unexpected/surprising/counterintuitive relative to what one would predict, and gives the specific detail of what was surprising. A 10: abstract uses explicit surprise framing (e.g., 'unexpected,' 'remarkably,' 'intriguing') tied to a concrete, specific counterintuitive detail. A 0: all findings are presented as expected/confirmatory with no surprise framing.
proposals.rationale: R15 (Intriguing Properties of Adversarial Training at Scale) explicitly frames 'one unexpected observation' (removing clean images boosts adversarial robustness by 18.3%); R48 (Words in Motion) states 'Remarkably, such modifications preserve the feasibility of predictions.' Both dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Abstract length / verbosity
proposals.instruction: On a scale of 0 (extremely terse, a few short sentences) to 10 (extremely long and verbose, many sentences with elaborate qualification), rate how LONG and VERBOSE the abstract text is -- word count, sentence count, and density of qualifying/elaborating clauses. Score only the extent of length/verbosity; do not judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the paper is good.
proposals.rationale: Sheer length/verbosity is a stylistic and space-allocation choice, not a measure of the underlying contribution: R43 (dense_pct=.999) states its whole idea in about three terse sentences, while R33 and R08 run many sentences of elaboration; a scorer that rewards elaboration would systematically favor the latter regardless of whether the terse item is actually the stronger piece of research.

proposals.name: Density of explicit numeric/percentage claims
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how densely the abstract is populated with explicit numeric performance figures (percentages, point-improvements, benchmark scores, speedup factors, e.g. '69.7%', '4.5x', '11.4%'). 0 = no numeric claims at all, 10 = numeric figures appear in nearly every sentence. Score only how MUCH such numeric claim-density is present in the text, not whether the numbers reported are impressive or credible.
proposals.rationale: Packing many explicit percentage/figure claims into the abstract is a reporting-style choice that can pad an abstract with cherry-picked numbers; R33 (92.7%, 28.5%, 49.5%) and R24 (69.7%) both saturate their abstracts with such figures while items like R43 or R29 report none, so a scorer keyed to numeric density would track this reporting habit rather than research quality.

proposals.name: Branded acronym title with colon subtitle
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the TITLE follows a 'branded acronym/name, followed by colon, followed by descriptive subtitle' convention (e.g., 'LOKI: A Comprehensive ...', 'EPISODE: Episodic ...'). 0 = plain descriptive title with no coined name, 10 = a fully coined acronym/brand name plus colon-subtitle. Score only the presence of this title-typography convention; do not judge whether the name is fitting or the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Coining a brand-name acronym and using a 'NAME: subtitle' title (R01 'EPISODE:', R08 'LOKI:') is a naming/marketing convention some authors adopt and others do not (e.g., R29's plain 'An Agnostic View on...'); it can inflate perceived memorability/credibility independent of the work's actual contribution.

proposals.name: Inline named-citation density in the abstract
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how densely the abstract text cites specific prior works inline by author-name-and-year (e.g., '(Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015)', 'Mallinar et al. 2022'). 0 = no inline named citations, 10 = many inline named citations woven through multiple sentences. Score only the extent of this citation-apparatus presence in the text, not whether the citations are apt or whether the paper is good.
proposals.rationale: Weaving inline author-year citations through the abstract itself, rather than reserving citation to a reference list, is a stylistic tic more common among authors steeped in a citation-heavy theoretical subfield; R06 and R18 both cite five-plus named prior works inline, which can read as more 'authoritative' to a criterion-based judge without reflecting the current paper's own contribution.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's seniority / disciplinary citation practice in this subfield

proposals.name: Enumerated contribution-list scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract uses explicit enumerated scaffolding markers to structure its content -- words/numerals like 'First,... Second,... Third,...', 'Firstly ... Finally', or '(1) ... (2) ... (3)'. 0 = no such enumerated markers, 10 = the abstract is built almost entirely around an explicit numbered/ordinal list structure. Score only the presence of this structural device, not whether the listed contributions are actually good or numerous.
proposals.rationale: Explicit enumerated scaffolding ('First,... Second,... Third...' in R38; '(1) Efficacy... (2) Retention' in R59) is a template an author either has or hasn't adopted for structuring an abstract; it can make contributions look more numerous/organized to a criterion-scoring judge while conveying no more actual content than an unstructured paragraph making the same points.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's template/practice habit in this submission format

proposals.name: Code/model release URL boilerplate sentence
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract contains an explicit boilerplate sentence announcing a code, model, or data release with a URL or platform name (e.g., 'Code is available at https://...', 'released on Github'). 0 = no such sentence, 10 = an unambiguous, prominent release-announcement sentence with a link. Score only whether/how prominently this boilerplate appears, not whether the released artifact is useful or the work is good.
proposals.rationale: A boilerplate 'code/data available at URL' sentence, present in both R06 and R44, signals engineering/release practice and lab resourcing rather than the quality of the scientific contribution; its mere presence can read as a rigor/credibility signal to a checklist-style judge independent of what the method actually contributes.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's/lab's institutional practice and resourcing for packaging code releases

proposals.name: Density of current LLM/agent/benchmark trend vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how densely the abstract uses current large-language-model-era trend vocabulary and named contemporary systems/benchmarks (e.g., 'LLM(s)', 'agent(s)', 'GPT', 'benchmark', a coined *Bench name). 0 = no such vocabulary, 10 = the abstract is saturated with this vocabulary throughout. Score only the density of this vocabulary, not whether the topic itself is important or the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Heavy use of current LLM/agent/benchmark vocabulary (R09's 'LLM agents'/'ProactiveBench', R38's 'LLMs'/'PERSONALITYBENCH') marks topical fashion and submission timing rather than the soundness of the contribution; a judge sensitive to trend vocabulary would over-reward being 'on-trend' regardless of whether the underlying idea is any good.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing within a topical fashion/hype cycle

proposals.name: Unhedged superlative/promotional adjective density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how densely the abstract uses unhedged superlative or promotional adverbs/adjectives (e.g., 'remarkably', 'significantly outperforms', 'notably', 'surprisingly', 'novel and comprehensive'). 0 = flat, unadorned reporting with no such language, 10 = the abstract is saturated with such promotional language. Score only the density of this promotional language, not whether the claims it dresses up are true or the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Adjectives like 'Remarkably' (R23) and phrasing like 'significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art' (R33) are self-promotional dressing that some authors apply liberally and others, e.g. R12's flat 'Here we show...', avoid entirely; this rhetorical habit can move a criterion-based judge's impression without reflecting any difference in the work itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's self-promotional practice developed through venue experience

proposals.name: Cross-topic recombination framing (trend A applied to domain B)
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how explicitly the abstract frames its contribution as importing an already-established technique/trend from one area into a different target domain (phrases like 'inspired by the success of X in Y, we explore its potential in Z', or a method that visibly welds together two previously separate named techniques/domains). 0 = the work reads as addressing a single, self-contained problem in one area, 10 = the abstract explicitly presents itself as a combination/transplantation of an established trend into a new domain. Score only the presence of this recombination framing, not whether the combination is a good idea or well executed.
proposals.rationale: Explicitly importing an established trend into a new domain -- R56 ('Inspired by the superior performance...of language-driven representation learning in centralized settings, we explore its potential to enhance FL') and R52's fusion of cuneiform paleography with modern generative image priors -- is a framing choice reflecting where in the topical cycle the item was written, since recombination becomes available only once each parent trend is already established, not a direct measure of how good the specific execution is.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the topical cycle (late entrant recombining already-established trends)

proposals.name: Reflective/critique-of-trend rhetorical framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract frames itself as a reflective, skeptical, or corrective commentary on an already-established recent trend or method family, rather than as a first, straightforward proposal -- look for cues like an interrogative or 'is X a free lunch'-style title, 'despite the popularity of X, there is limited understanding...', or explicit language of 'revisiting', 'deconstructing', or 'rekindling interest in' prior approaches. 0 = the abstract reads as a first straightforward proposal with no such reflective framing, 10 = the abstract is explicitly organized around questioning/deconstructing/revisiting an established trend. Score only the presence of this rhetorical framing, not whether the critique is correct or the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Framing an abstract as a corrective/reflective commentary on an existing trend -- R24's interrogative 'Is Factuality Enhancement a Free Lunch For LLMs?' and R30's explicit 'deconstruct...rekindle interest in a family of classical methods' -- can only be written once the trend it critiques already has enough prior, 'obvious-take' submissions to react against; it is a positional/rhetorical tell about when-in-the-stream the item arrives, not a measure of the work's own soundness.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (late-arriving reflective/critical riff after early obvious takes)

proposals.name: Mechanistic explanatory chain
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives a specific, coherent chain from the problem mechanism through the proposed design to the expected effect; score 0 when it only names a method and reports improvement without explaining why it should work.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R45 connect training behavior to precise dynamical explanations, while R30 and R41 link observed failures to concrete normalization or representation mechanisms.

proposals.name: Problem-solution fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each major design choice directly addresses a clearly diagnosed obstacle in the target problem; score 0 when the method appears generic or its components are weakly connected to the stated challenge.
proposals.rationale: R32 maps foreground imbalance and pixel relations to two targeted distillation mechanisms, and R37 maps compounding skill-chain errors to mobile skills and region goals.

proposals.name: Structure-matched inductive bias
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the model architecture or objective encodes a meaningful structure intrinsic to the data or task; score 0 when it treats structured inputs as generic vectors without a task-specific bias.
proposals.rationale: R02 models time-varying sensor dependencies, R47 represents directional long-range interactions, and R52 introduces higher-order attention for logical relations.

proposals.name: Conceptual sharpness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract makes a precise conceptual distinction, formalizes it clearly, and derives a non-obvious method or insight from that distinction; score 0 when the contribution is described only as a vague improvement or collection of standard components.
proposals.rationale: R10 reframes learned Bloom-filter utilization as an optimization problem, R16 distinguishes multisets from sets, and R60 defines overfitting cost in a deliberately agnostic way.

proposals.name: Essential-component isolation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work systematically identifies which components are necessary, sufficient, or redundant through decomposition or ablation; score 0 when the abstract presents a bundled system without isolating contributors.
proposals.rationale: R19 deconstructs diffusion models to identify essential representation-learning components, while R31 reports module-level ablations and R38 diagnoses separate memory defects before proposing fixes.

proposals.name: Controlled diagnostic evaluation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when experiments use controlled comparisons, perturbations, or matched alternatives that isolate the claimed mechanism; score 0 when evaluation consists only of aggregate benchmark comparisons.
proposals.rationale: R23 uses counterfactually revised documents, R28 tests logically matched but visually different tasks, and R30 separates clean/adversarial normalization effects.

proposals.name: Meaningful-shift generalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract tests transfer to genuinely unseen sensors, tasks, domains, poses, operating points, or distributions that probe the stated capability; score 0 when all evidence comes from the same narrow setting as training.
proposals.rationale: R02 includes leave-sensor-out settings, R48 tests unseen human actions and black-box detectors, and R49 evaluates operating points not used during training.

proposals.name: Assumption and boundary transparency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states important assumptions and characterizes where guarantees or behavior hold and fail; score 0 when claims are presented without conditions, limitations, or scope boundaries.
proposals.rationale: R09 explicitly targets general sources using only i.i.d. samples, R17 distinguishes label-aware from label-agnostic robustness, and R60 analyzes targets outside the RKHS and finite-sample regimes.

proposals.name: Uncertainty-aware decision design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when uncertainty is estimated meaningfully and directly controls conservative behavior, extrapolation, or trust in model predictions; score 0 when uncertainty is absent or mentioned only as an unvalidated auxiliary output.
proposals.rationale: R20 detects out-of-distribution molecules, R55 trades model-based and model-free estimates using epistemic uncertainty, and R58 uses energy margins for graph OOD detection.

proposals.name: Compositional representation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the representation explicitly separates factors and recombines them to support interpretable control, novel combinations, or transfer; score 0 when representations remain entangled and are used only for one fixed prediction task.
proposals.rationale: R15 extracts opposing-feature directions for controllable motion changes, R27 composes interests from multiple item facets, and R49 parameterizes solutions by preference vectors.

proposals.name: Theory-experiment alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal analysis predicts or explains concrete design choices and empirical patterns that are then tested; score 0 when theory and experiments are disconnected or theoretical claims are merely decorative.
proposals.rationale: R13 connects supervision complexity to teacher accuracy, margins, temperature, and online distillation, while R53 derives its federated algorithm from relaxed-smoothness analysis and tests the resulting complexity claims.

proposals.name: Efficiency-quality integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when resource savings are quantified together with preservation or improvement of the task capability, including relevant end-to-end costs; score 0 when efficiency is asserted without accounting or quality evidence.
proposals.rationale: R06 ties batch scaling to training time without accuracy degradation, R22 quantifies training-time reduction and accuracy, and R24 connects extreme quantization to single-GPU inference and measured speedups.

proposals.name: Evaluation construct validity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the dataset, metric, and protocol directly measure the phenomenon claimed, including appropriate granularity and human or expert grounding where needed; score 0 when the evaluation proxy is weakly related to the claim.
proposals.rationale: R01 spans modalities, difficulty levels, anomaly localization, and explanations, R21 validates implicitness against human judgments, and R51 uses expert cuneiform annotations for fine-grained structure.

proposals.name: Failure-mode-targeted intervention
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mode and introduces an intervention whose operation is visibly tailored to that failure; score 0 when the proposed change is generic and no failure mechanism is specified.
proposals.rationale: R38 identifies noisy addressing, aliasing, and linkage degradation before introducing corresponding memory fixes, while R42 targets distribution conflict in offline RL with a behavior-model prior.

proposals.name: Extensible method interface
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the contribution is presented as a reusable module, framework, or interface that naturally applies across architectures, tasks, or problem instances; score 0 when it is tightly specialized to one dataset, model, or pipeline with no evident reuse path.
proposals.rationale: R35 describes embedding and matching mechanisms reusable as plugins, R47 emphasizes integration with fields and fast multipole methods, and R16 improves an existing set-prediction network through a broadly applicable optimization technique.

proposals.name: Acronym and method-brand density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract contains newly coined acronyms, branded method names, or stylized capitalization; judge only visible naming density, not whether the method is good.
proposals.rationale: Distinctive naming can reflect practiced conference packaging and memorability rather than research quality. Examples include R06 UV-Attack, R13 WavTokenizer, R23 EPISODE, and R54 CBOP.

proposals.name: Quantified performance emphasis
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract foregrounds exact percentages, speedups, rankings, or numerical comparisons; do not judge whether the numbers are impressive or credible.
proposals.rationale: Numerical emphasis may attract text models through salience and specificity while reflecting persuasive style rather than quality. Examples include R06's 92.7% and 49.5% figures, R25's 76 minutes, and R58's 3.25x and 4.5x speedups.

proposals.name: External-resource boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract includes code, data, model-weight, project-page, or repository-availability language and links; do not judge whether the resources are useful.
proposals.rationale: Open-resource language can be a lab or community practice that affects textual reception independently of the scientific contribution, while also plausibly correlating with genuine quality. Examples include R02, R05, R10, R13, and R49.

proposals.name: Technical notation density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of inline mathematics, LaTeX notation, symbols, named losses, and formal technical expressions; judge only quantity and visual prominence, not rigor.
proposals.rationale: Notation-heavy prose may act as a sophistication cue learned from community style, without itself establishing quality. Examples include R01's repeated operator notation, R18's coreset formulas, and R56's kernel-regression terminology.

proposals.name: Promotional novelty language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of self-certifying language such as “novel,” “first,” “remarkably,” “significantly,” “state-of-the-art,” or “unprecedented”; do not judge whether any claim is deserved.
proposals.rationale: Promotional phrasing is a rhetorical habit that can trigger model responses independently of research quality. Examples include R06, R13, R24, R36, and R50.

proposals.name: Prestige-reference concentration
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract relies on recognizable model, dataset, benchmark, institution, or named-baseline references; do not judge the importance of the referenced entities.
proposals.rationale: Recognizable names can exploit shared audience familiarity and community signaling rather than indicate contribution quality. Examples include R19's miniImageNet/CUB-200/CIFAR-100 references, R25's BERT and ResNet-50, and R41's GPT-4 and commercial-model comparisons.

proposals.name: Temporal fashion markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the abstract uses rapidly changing topical markers such as LLMs, diffusion, NeRF, GPT, or current model versions; judge only topical recency signals, not scientific relevance.
proposals.rationale: Topical fashion can influence model expectations through recency cues while being orthogonal to intrinsic quality. Examples include R03, R06, R29, R41, R42, and R50.

proposals.name: Template-shaped checklist structure
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract follows a visibly formulaic sequence of problem, numbered contributions, modules, experiments, and availability claims; do not judge whether the structure communicates well.
proposals.rationale: Rubric-shaped structure may be optimized for predictable processing and can correlate with experienced writing, but the structure itself is not quality. Examples include R06's staged solution description, R13's numbered advantages, and R33's explicit framework-component sequence.
proposals.upstream_parent: receiving-side rubric and author template practice

proposals.name: Submission-editing residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for visible formatting residue such as broken URLs, awkward line wrapping, hyphenation artifacts, duplicated text, malformed LaTeX, or inconsistent spacing; do not judge what caused the residue.
proposals.rationale: Editing or deadline artifacts can leave text fingerprints that models may associate with particular submission processes without reflecting research quality. Examples include R15's “task un- certainty,” R32's duplicated malformed GitHub link, R38's broken line layout, and R49's “sur- rounding.”

proposals.name: Obvious-versus-late-riff framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract reads as a direct, conventional response to a familiar prompt rather than a layered reinterpretation, contrarian reframing, or second-order extension; judge only textual framing, not originality or quality.
proposals.rationale: An early or crowded-stream position could encourage obvious framing, while later entries may visibly riff on established formulations; the textual trace is framing style, not quality. Examples include the direct diagnostic framing in R04 and R38 versus the second-order reframings in R03 and R21.

proposals.name: Bottleneck–mechanism alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mode and introduces a mechanism that directly addresses it with an explicit causal connection; score 0 when the proposed method has no clear relation to the stated bottleneck.
proposals.rationale: R51 separates normalization effects from capacity effects in adversarial training, while R55 targets foreground imbalance and missing spatial relations in distillation.

proposals.name: Cross-regime conceptual unification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one clearly stated principle explains or supports behavior across substantially different tasks, domains, or operating conditions; score 0 when the contribution is confined to one narrow setting without a unifying idea.
proposals.rationale: R01 meta-learns curiosity algorithms across diverse control domains, while R45 unifies directional, long-range, external-field, and fast-multipole interactions.

proposals.name: Theory–experiment agreement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal analysis yields predictions or explanations that are directly tested by experiments; score 0 when theoretical claims and empirical demonstrations are largely disconnected.
proposals.rationale: R04 constructs a toy dynamics whose rigorous analysis explains observed edge-of-stability behavior, and R52 links supervision-complexity theory to online-distillation experiments.

proposals.name: Diagnostic component attribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract isolates which components, assumptions, or interventions cause the observed behavior and explains why; score 0 when it reports only aggregate performance of an opaque bundle.
proposals.rationale: R18 progressively removes diffusion components to identify what representation learning actually needs, while R32 analyzes hidden states and logits to explain a factuality–context tradeoff.

proposals.name: Evaluation coverage of claims
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the evaluation directly tests each major claimed capability using complementary datasets, metrics, conditions, or baselines; score 0 when broad claims rest on one generic experiment or metric.
proposals.rationale: R12 evaluates multimodal synthetic-data detection through multiple task types and difficulty levels, while R14 combines formal coreset guarantees, datasets, baselines, and downstream speed tests.

proposals.name: Out-of-distribution robustness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract explicitly tests conditions unlike training data and demonstrates behavior under meaningful shifts, unseen cases, or missing inputs; score 0 when evaluation is limited to ordinary in-distribution testing.
proposals.rationale: R21 tests unseen human poses and black-box detectors, and R28 evaluates leave-sensor-out settings for irregularly sampled time series.

proposals.name: Task-matched structural bias
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the architecture or representation encodes the task’s relevant geometry, hierarchy, symmetry, or compositional structure and the connection is explained; score 0 when the architecture is generic with no task-specific structural rationale.
proposals.rationale: R10 introduces higher-order attention for logical reasoning, while R30 uses hyperbolic geometry for hierarchical linguistic structure.

proposals.name: Resource–quality tradeoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract quantifies substantial compute, memory, energy, storage, or communication savings while measuring the associated capability preservation or loss; score 0 when resource implications are ignored or only asserted vaguely.
proposals.rationale: R13 connects bit pruning to an explicit accuracy–energy tradeoff, while R38 quantifies embedding compression alongside accuracy degradation.

proposals.name: Modular reuse and transfer
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the proposed component has a clear interface, improves multiple existing systems, or transfers across tasks and compositions; score 0 when it is tightly coupled to one task with no reuse pathway.
proposals.rationale: R22 presents embedding and masking contributions as reusable plugins, while R59 designs mobile skills and region goals to compose across long-horizon manipulation tasks.

proposals.name: Uncertainty-aware conservatism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method represents relevant uncertainty and uses it to alter inference, optimization, or decisions conservatively; score 0 when uncertain and reliable cases are treated identically.
proposals.rationale: R35 explicitly trades model-based and model-free estimates according to epistemic uncertainty, while R33 uses energy margins to detect graph out-of-distribution samples.

proposals.name: Representation fidelity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract tests whether learned representations preserve the intended semantics, structure, or causal feature under controlled perturbations or transfers; score 0 when representation quality is inferred only from an unrelated task metric.
proposals.rationale: R24 tests transfer of implicit logical structure across visually dissimilar tasks, while R54 probes whether language and visual representations share the claimed semantic structure.

proposals.name: Measurement and benchmark validity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the task, annotations, difficulty variation, and metrics are clearly tied to the scientific construct and include credible independent or expert validation; score 0 when measurement is weakly defined or relies only on an unvalidated proxy.
proposals.rationale: R12 builds a multimodal benchmark with curated questions, difficulty levels, and fine-grained explanations, while R53 introduces expert annotations for a specialized paleographic task.

proposals.name: Post-training flexibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one trained system supports adjustable preferences, arbitrary resolutions, new operating points, or rapid knowledge updates with predictable behavior; score 0 when every new condition requires separate retraining or a fixed configuration.
proposals.rationale: R37 selects new Pareto operating points after training, while R60 generates arbitrary-sized images using a single patch-based framework.

proposals.name: Boundary-condition honesty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract explicitly identifies limitations, failures, tradeoffs, or applicability boundaries and investigates them; score 0 when it presents only universal success claims without scope or negative evidence.
proposals.rationale: R24 reports failures on implicit logic despite partial structural transfer, and R32 documents that factuality enhancement can substantially harm context-faithfulness.

proposals.name: Principled simplification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work removes complexity or parameters, demonstrates that the retained mechanism suffices, and explains why omitted components are unnecessary; score 0 when it merely adds modules without necessity evidence.
proposals.rationale: R18 shows that many diffusion components are nonessential for representation learning, while R20 argues that a large learned classifier can be fixed with little loss.

proposals.name: Contribution stacking
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses densely packed, numbered, multi-part contribution claims; do not judge whether the contributions are good or important.
proposals.rationale: R04 and R31 stack several named contributions and capabilities into long enumerations, creating a recognizable presentation pattern independent of research quality.

proposals.name: Numerical spectacle
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract foregrounds exact percentages, speedups, benchmark gains, or superlative comparisons; do not judge whether the numbers are credible or valuable.
