proposals.rationale: R07, R13, and R42 prominently feature precise gains and dramatic runtime comparisons, a reporting style plausibly shaped by persuasive audience expectations rather than quality alone.

proposals.name: Acronym branding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract introduces invented method, dataset, benchmark, or framework names and capitalized acronyms; do not judge whether the names are useful or the methods are good.
proposals.rationale: R03 introduces LOKI, R10 introduces EPISODE, and R35 introduces UV-Attack, showing strong branded-nomenclature fingerprints associated with format familiarity.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the conference format

proposals.name: Reproducibility signposting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract advertises code, data, checkpoints, project pages, or public implementation links; do not judge whether the release is complete or beneficial.
proposals.rationale: R13, R22, and R35 explicitly advertise implementation or project resources, a textual trace of release practice that may correlate with genuine engineering quality but is not itself quality.

proposals.name: Canonical anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract anchors its story in named models, established benchmarks, named techniques, or parenthetical literature citations; do not judge whether the references are appropriate or insightful.
proposals.rationale: R08 names CLIP and cognitive-science constructs, while R50 invokes BERT, Poincare probes, and multiple probing traditions; such citation anchoring can reflect community positioning as well as substance.

proposals.name: Formalism density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract contains equations, mathematical symbols, theorem-like claims, asymptotic notation, or proof-oriented language; do not judge whether the mathematics is correct or rigorous.
proposals.rationale: R02 uses sharpness equations and rigorous-region language, while R23 and R37 use formal risk definitions and asymptotic bounds; mathematical presentation style can influence reception apart from quality.

proposals.name: Scope breadth
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract claims coverage across multiple domains, modalities, datasets, tasks, or application areas; do not judge whether the breadth is useful or convincingly demonstrated.
proposals.rationale: R03 spans video, image, 3D, text, and audio, while R06 combines chemical, geometric, physical, and conformational aspects; broad packaging can affect reception independently of research quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience targeting and author packaging practice

proposals.name: Promotional boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses stock phrases such as “novel,” “comprehensive,” “state-of-the-art,” “significantly,” “remarkably,” or “paves the way”; do not judge whether the claims deserve those words.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R60 repeatedly use formulaic novelty, comprehensive-scope, and future-impact language, while R20 adds “remarkably” and state-of-the-art phrasing.

proposals.name: Late-riff positioning
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract reads as a late-arriving synthesis or gap-filling response, with extended contrasts among many existing methods and carefully enumerated limitations; do not judge whether the response is original or good.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R55 spend substantial space mapping existing approaches, their limitations, and a targeted corrective proposal; this textual stance could be associated with submission order even though actual position is unseen.

proposals.name: Formatting residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract contains extraction, editing, or layout artifacts such as broken hyphenation, irregular spacing, bullet fragments, malformed URLs, or inconsistent TeX formatting; do not judge whether the underlying work is good.
proposals.rationale: R18 contains broken lineation and hyphenation, R19 has fragmented words, and R34 includes a malformed duplicated URL, leaving visible process fingerprints unrelated to research quality.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Justification over Empirical Metrics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract deeply explains the underlying mechanism of why a method works or identifies a specific causal component driving performance. Score 0 if the abstract solely reports performance metrics (e.g., accuracy, speedup) without any mechanistic explanation.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values understanding why a method works over sheer empirical gains, as seen in R43 (diagnosing BN) and R45 (deconstructing DDMs), whereas it discounts pure SOTA-chasing in R09 (WizardMath) and R29 (OPTQ).

proposals.name: Novel Conceptual Reframing of Problem
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper fundamentally redefines an existing problem or formulation, making previously intractable issues naturally dissolve. Score 0 if the paper addresses a problem using the exact same formulation as prior work, merely applying a new algorithm.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts like R18 (multiset vs set) and R39 (fixing the classifier) succeed by reframing the problem, unlike dense-disfavored R26 (applying ETFs to FSCIL) and R07 (standard Pareto front optimization).

proposals.name: Elegant Simplification or Deconstructive Insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reveals that a complex modern system can be replaced by a much simpler, classical, or minimalist approach without loss of efficacy. Score 0 if the abstract achieves its results by adding complex modules, extra loss terms, or heavy engineering on top of existing pipelines.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high papers often strip away complexity to find core truths (R45, R39, R10), while dense-low papers tend to add complexity via heavy pipelines (R03, R59).

proposals.name: Clear Translation of Theory to Practice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract presents a rigorous theoretical result (e.g., bounds, proofs) and clearly translates it into actionable algorithmic insights or practical guidelines. Score 0 if the abstract presents purely empirical results or abstract theory with no practical translation.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high papers like R34 (cost of overfitting) and R27 (near-optimal coresets) bridge theory and practice elegantly, whereas dense-low papers like R15 (exponential LR) or R52 (LAMB) lack this tight theoretical-practical feedback loop.

proposals.name: Identification of Flaws in Standard Paradigms
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract pinpoints a subtle but critical flaw, contradiction, or limitation in a widely accepted standard method or evaluation metric. Score 0 if the abstract accepts standard baselines and methods as flawless, simply proposing an alternative.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors papers that critically examine standard tools (R18 set-equivariance, R43 BN in adversarial training, R37 KD understanding), unlike dense-low papers that build on top of standards without questioning them (R32, R50).

proposals.name: Methodological Minimalism vs System Engineering
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the proposed method achieves its goals through a highly targeted, minimal, and elegant intervention. Score 0 if the proposed method is a complex pipeline, an ensemble of techniques, or a large-scale engineering effort.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high abstracts favor elegant, targeted interventions (R28 energy extraction, R57 ABM prior), while dense-low abstracts often feature heavy engineering pipelines (R08 LOKI benchmark, R49 LLM fusion).

proposals.name: Novel Algorithmic or Geometric Primitive
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core contribution is a brand new, fundamental mathematical or algorithmic building block (e.g., a new operator, geometric space, or attention mechanism). Score 0 if the core contribution is a recombination of existing algorithms, a new loss function variant, or a benchmark.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored papers introduce new primitives (R40 2-simplicial transformer, R12 Cartesian multipoles), whereas dense-disfavored ones rely on existing primitives or datasets (R05 ProactiveBench, R36 PersonalityBench).

proposals.name: Explicit Analysis of Fundamental Trade-offs
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract rigorously explores and quantifies a fundamental trade-off (e.g., accuracy vs. robustness, exploration vs. exploitation) rather than ignoring it. Score 0 if the abstract claims universal improvement across all metrics without discussing any inherent trade-offs.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high papers explicitly model trade-offs (R20 model-free vs model-based uncertainty, R34 benign vs catastrophic overfitting), while dense-low papers claim 'free lunch' or universal gains (R29 OPTQ, R54 FedGLCL).

proposals.name: Integration of Discrete and Continuous Mathematics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method effectively bridges discrete and continuous mathematical spaces (e.g., combinatorial structures and continuous optimization). Score 0 if the method operates entirely within a single mathematical domain without bridging gaps.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high abstracts often combine discrete and continuous concepts elegantly (R11 flow matching and Markov bridges, R10 bit-pruning continuous weights to discrete bits), a property lacking in dense-low papers (R21 InfinityGAN, R42 hyperbolic probing).

proposals.name: Justified Structural Inductive Bias
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract introduces a specific, well-justified structural inductive bias that maps directly to the underlying physics, logic, or geometry of the problem. Score 0 if the architecture is a generic black-box model with no problem-specific inductive biases.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high papers use strong, justified inductive biases (R12 anisotropic state for electrostatics, R40 tensor products for logic, R14 Bayes-Adaptive task uncertainty), while dense-low papers rely more on generic scaling (R09 WizardMath, R15 exponential LR).

proposals.name: Explicit Epistemic Uncertainty Modeling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method explicitly models, quantifies, or relies on epistemic uncertainty, task ambiguity, or model confidence in its core algorithm. Score 0 if the method treats the model as a deterministic black box without any measure of uncertainty.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high abstracts incorporate epistemic uncertainty centrally (R20 CBOP uncertainty bounds, R11 DrugFlow OOD estimates, R56 label uncertainty), unlike dense-low abstracts (R03 WavTokenizer, R29 OPTQ).

proposals.name: Investigation of Fundamental Limits / Boundaries
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper studies what is mathematically possible, optimal, or fundamentally bounded in a learning problem. Score 0 if the paper focuses only on pushing empirical performance higher without investigating theoretical limits.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored papers investigate fundamental boundaries (R06 R-D sandwich bounds, R27 near-optimal coresets, R34 cost of overfitting), unlike dense-disfavored empirical pushes (R52 LAMB training speed, R07 Pareto front).

proposals.name: Orthogonal Contribution over Incremental SOTA
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the proposed capability is orthogonal to existing methods, offering a fundamentally new axis of improvement or a new task formulation. Score 0 if the paper directly competes with prior work on the exact same axis, aiming only to incrementally beat SOTA.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high abstracts offer orthogonal value (R48 task decomposition from demonstration, R22 interpretable control vectors), while dense-low abstracts focus on direct incremental SOTA (R32 KD for object detection, R55 GAN steerability).

proposals.name: Generality via Abstract Mathematical Formulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core contribution is framed in highly abstract mathematical terms that apply to a broad class of problems beyond the specific experiments shown. Score 0 if the method is heavily tailored to a specific application domain, dataset, or architecture.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high abstracts derive abstract formulations (R27 robust clustering formulation, R34 KRR overfitting), whereas dense-low abstracts are tied closely to specific applications (R44 cuneiform signs, R16 UV-attack).

proposals.name: Scientific Insight vs Benchmark Creation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract derives deep scientific or mechanistic insight from careful experimental design, using models as tools for understanding. Score 0 if the primary contribution is the creation of a new dataset, benchmark, or leaderboard to rank models.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high abstracts prioritize scientific insight (R45 deconstructing DDMs, R43 diagnosing BN), while dense-low abstracts focus heavily on benchmark creation and leaderboards (R08 LOKI, R05 ProactiveBench).

proposals.name: Prominent system acronym
proposals.instruction: Score from 0-10 the extent to which the abstract introduces and repeatedly emphasizes a specific, catchy acronym or branded system name (e.g., OPTQ, LOKI, WavTokenizer). 0 means no specific name/acronym is used; 10 means a named system dominates the text. Do not judge if this is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Catchy acronyms often act as a branding artifact that scorecard models might mistakenly score as concreteness or significance. In this slice, R10 (EPISODE), R11 (LOKI), and R46 (WizardMath) heavily rely on branded system names, whereas dense-high items like R13 and R20 simply describe the mathematical or conceptual method.

proposals.name: Hype paradigm keyword density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text relies heavily on current, highly hyped paradigm keywords (e.g., 'LLM', 'Large Language Model', 'NeRF', 'GPT', 'Diffusion', 'agents'). 0 means no hyped keywords; 10 means the abstract is saturated with them. Do not judge whether the use is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Papers submitted during the peak of a hype cycle may receive inflated scores from rigid criteria impressed by trendy keywords, independent of underlying quality. R17, R32, R46, and R54 are saturated with LLM/agent buzzwords, while dense-high items like R02 and R13 completely avoid them.

proposals.name: Extreme compute scale mention
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract explicitly mentions massive scales of compute, parameters, or datasets (e.g., '175 billion parameters', 'TPUv3 Pod', '18K questions'). 0 means no mentions of extreme scale; 10 means extreme scale is a central focus. Do not judge whether the scale is impressive.
proposals.rationale: Well-resourced labs can train or evaluate on massive scales, leaving a textual fingerprint of extreme dataset/compute sizes that reads as impressive without denoting fundamental theoretical quality. R11, R19, and R34 lean heavily on extreme scale mentions, unlike dense-high theoretical or methodological papers like R05 and R13.
proposals.upstream_parent: authorship by well-resourced lab / big tech

proposals.name: Contribution boilerplate density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract uses highly templated, boilerplate phrases to introduce contributions (e.g., 'In this paper, we propose', 'Specifically, we introduce', 'We present X, a novel'). 0 means no boilerplate; 10 means every contribution is introduced with rigid templates. Do not judge if this is good writing.
proposals.rationale: Formulaic transitions are often a product of heavy editing or extensive practice with the submission format, which can trick a scorecard into perceiving high structural clarity. R14, R15, and R34 use rigid templates ('In this paper, we introduce X, a novel...'), whereas dense-high papers like R02 and R49 adopt more natural, direct phrasing.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format / templated assistance

proposals.name: Reactive incremental framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract reads as a late-stage, reactive combination of existing popular frameworks, heavily referencing 'recent' works and framing itself as an incremental step over them. 0 means entirely foundational; 10 means a purely reactive combination of recent trends. Do not judge if the step is good.
proposals.rationale: An abstract that enters a saturated conversation late often frames itself reactively (e.g., 'recent advances in X suggest...'). R14, R17, and R46 read as late-arriving riffs on existing paradigms, while dense-high items like R04, R13, and R30 establish foundational problems from scratch, suggesting a difference in submission timing and awareness of the crowd.

proposals.name: Unverified metric boasting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text lists multiple highly specific, large percentage improvements or raw metric spikes (e.g., '92.7% attack success rate', '69.7% decrease', '116.4%') without defining them. 0 means no raw metric drops; 10 means the text is cluttered with raw percentages. Do not judge the validity of the metrics.
proposals.rationale: Papers attempting to compensate for a lack of deep insight often flood the abstract with uncontextualized, highly specific metric improvements to impress checklist-based reviewers. R09, R17, R19, and R21 feature raw metric dumps, whereas dense-high papers like R05 and R25 emphasize conceptual findings over raw numbers.

proposals.name: Application utility focus
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract frames its primary value around a specific, immediate practical application (e.g., object detection, drug design, cuneiform signs) rather than general methodological or theoretical advances. 0 means purely theoretical; 10 means entirely application-driven. Do not judge the application's usefulness.
proposals.rationale: Application-driven research often emphasizes domain utility (fueled by industry or specific grants) over fundamental machine learning insights, which can bias a scorecard if the criteria value practicality. R09, R22, and R43 focus purely on hyper-specific applications, unlike dense-high items like R13, R31, and R41 which target broad methodological gaps.

proposals.name: Prominent code link
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract features a prominent, fully formatted URL, GitHub link, or project page. 0 means no link; 10 means a highly prominent link taking up text space. Do not judge if the link is good.
proposals.rationale: The presence of a raw URL is a formatting choice that may inadvertently inflate a scorecard's rating for 'reproducibility' or 'open science' criteria regardless of actual research quality. Dense-low items like R09, R10, R11, and R15 explicitly include GitHub links, while dense-high items like R04, R13, and R49 omit them entirely.

proposals.name: Rhetorical question hook
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract or title uses a rhetorical question to hook the reader (e.g., 'Is generative modeling... solved?', 'Can artificial agents learn...?'). 0 means no questions; 10 means the entire premise is posed as a question. Do not judge if this is engaging.
proposals.rationale: Using a rhetorical question is a narrative gimmick often used to artificially heighten the perceived importance of a problem. R03, R17, R28, and R33 employ this trope heavily in their titles or openings, a stylistic choice entirely absent from the dense-high items like R30.

proposals.name: Broad accessibility narrative
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the abstract uses plain-English, highly accessible analogies or explicitly states its goal to be simple/understandable (e.g., 'philosophy is to deconstruct', 'in plain English'). 0 means highly technical jargon; 10 means heavily simplified narrative. Do not judge if accessibility is good.
proposals.rationale: Authors targeting a broad, non-specialist audience (or writing for a general press release) often simplify their narrative and explicitly state their goal to be accessible, which scorecards might reward as 'clarity'. R05 and R11 use accessible, sweeping language, whereas dense-high papers like R13, R30, and R49 lean into dense, specialized terminology.

proposals.name: Theoretical Primacy over Empirical Engineering
proposals.instruction: 10 = introduces a fundamentally new mathematical or conceptual paradigm, deriving properties from first principles; 0 = applies engineering heuristics to standard tasks without deep theoretical grounding.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly ranks abstracts introducing new theories (R16, R57, R23) while the scorecard over-credits empirical scaling and benchmark creations (R58, R50).

proposals.name: Deconstructive Analysis Together With Mechanistic Insight
proposals.instruction: 10 = provides deep mechanistic understanding by isolating components or probing latent spaces to explain how models work; 0 = treats the model as a black box and reports only end-to-end performance metrics.
proposals.rationale: Explains the dense model's preference for mechanistic understanding (R10, R41, R19) over opaque, highly-tuned applied models (R13, R27).

proposals.name: Rigorous Mathematical Guarantees
proposals.instruction: 10 = explicitly states near-optimal theoretical bounds, formal proofs of convergence, or guaranteed margins; 0 = makes no formal mathematical claims, relying entirely on heuristic observations.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors rigorous theoretical bounds (R08, R44, R57), whereas the scorecard seems to miss this depth in favor of heuristic algorithmic tweaks (R45, R31).

proposals.name: Unifying Disparate Mathematical Frameworks
proposals.instruction: 10 = formally merges two or more distinct mathematical or algorithmic frameworks into a single cohesive theory; 0 = applies a single, standard algorithm to a new task.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts that integrate distinct theoretical frameworks score highly with the dense model (R04, R26, R07), a structural nuance the scorecard likely misses when preferring keyword-heavy applied papers (R37, R38).

proposals.name: High Conceptual Density Together With Zero Hyperbole
proposals.instruction: 10 = highly concise, mathematically dense abstract entirely devoid of marketing language or subjective superlatives; 0 = verbose, filled with buzzwords and broad qualitative claims without rigorous content.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors extremely dense, concise abstracts (R16, R57, R08), while the scorecard is apparently easily impressed by verbose, hyped-up abstracts (R13, R50, R58).

proposals.name: Identifying Fundamental Flaws Together With Mathematical Resolution
proposals.instruction: 10 = articulates a fundamental theoretical flaw or unrecognized paradox in widely-used methods and mathematically resolves it; 0 = identifies a minor empirical bug and provides an ad-hoc patch.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards the discovery of fundamental theoretical flaws (R39, R48, R17, R05), while the scorecard over-credits minor engineering bug fixes (R24, R34).

proposals.name: Principled Architectural Biases With Logical Grounding
proposals.instruction: 10 = introduces a new architectural inductive bias strictly derived from physical, geometric, or logical laws; 0 = uses standard architectures with ad-hoc tuning for a specific domain.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values principled inductive biases (R16, R53, R26), whereas the scorecard misses this depth, preferring standard architectures applied to new datasets (R56, R42).

proposals.name: Bayesian Frameworks Together With Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification
proposals.instruction: 10 = rigorously quantifies and acts upon epistemic uncertainty using formal Bayesian or model-based frameworks; 0 = uses heuristic rewards or ignores model uncertainty entirely.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors formal treatments of uncertainty (R30, R46, R09), while the scorecard misses this, instead rewarding heuristic or manually-derived reward systems (R60, R15).

proposals.name: Domain-Agnostic Formalism Generality
proposals.instruction: 10 = the proposed mathematical formalism or algorithm is demonstrated to be applicable across vastly different domains without domain-specific tweaks; 0 = hyper-tuned to a single narrow application.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly values formalism that proves general across disparate domains (R07, R28, R29), whereas the scorecard seems to prefer methods narrowly tailored to specific empirical tasks (R03, R27, R33).

proposals.name: Zero-Overhead Methods Together With Provable Guarantees
proposals.instruction: 10 = proves theoretical bounds or guarantees that require zero extra parameters or negligible computational overhead at inference; 0 = achieves empirical gains purely via massive compute or heavy parameterization.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors highly efficient, provably bounded methods (R08, R12, R28), while the scorecard overlooks the elegance of zero-overhead proofs in favor of compute-heavy empirical scaling (R58, R55).

proposals.name: Reframing Applied Problems Together With Fundamental Math
proposals.instruction: 10 = takes an applied problem and successfully recasts it into a fundamental mathematical framework (e.g., transport theory); 0 = solves an applied problem using off-the-shelf networks without formal reframing.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards the mathematical reframing of applied domains (R26, R08, R04), while the scorecard misses this conceptual leap and prefers standard applied heuristics (R36, R40).

proposals.name: Exposing Hidden Structural Limitations
proposals.instruction: 10 = mathematically proves that an existing popular model contains an unrecognized structural limitation (e.g., inability to represent multisets); 0 = simply observes an empirical failure on a benchmark.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly weights abstracts that formally expose hidden structural limits (R17, R41, R48), whereas the scorecard is drawn towards superficial empirical probing (R56, R43).

proposals.name: Physical Constraints Together With Formal Mathematical Rigor
proposals.instruction: 10 = perfectly aligns mathematical algorithms with exact physical, thermodynamic, or geometric laws; 0 = uses physics-based loss terms heuristically without formal mathematical alignment.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values the rigorous integration of physical laws with algorithms (R53, R26, R04), a nuanced composite quality the scorecard misses, instead favoring standard empirical applied physics tasks (R03, R40).

proposals.name: Causal Frameworks Together With Mechanistic Explanations
proposals.instruction: 10 = uses a causal or rigorous theoretical framework together with mechanistic analysis to explain exactly *why* a phenomenon occurs; 0 = simply observes *that* a phenomenon occurs empirically.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards deep causal/mechanistic explanations (R41, R22, R44), while the scorecard is satisfied by purely empirical observations of phenomena (R35, R38).

proposals.name: Information Bottlenecks Together With Provable Optimality
proposals.instruction: 10 = achieves sparsity, compression, or information bottlenecks strictly through mathematically proven optimality bounds; 0 = uses empirical pruning or quantization without theoretical motivation.
proposals.rationale: The dense model prefers theoretically grounded information bottlenecks (R08, R28, R12), while the scorecard overlooks the proof in favor of empirical compression methods (R54, R55).

proposals.name: Proprietary system and dataset branding
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the abstract introduces and repeatedly capitalizes a specific, branded name for the proposed method, architecture, or dataset (e.g., acronyms or portmanteaus like 'ProtoSnap', 'PERSONALITYBench'). Do not judge if the name is good or clever, only count the extent of branded proper nouns.
proposals.rationale: A feature-matching model often relies on explicit cues and may give high scores to texts that use catchy, branded acronyms. An end-to-end model focuses on semantics rather than branding. Seen prominently in R01, R02, and R60.

proposals.name: Extreme scale and competitor name-dropping
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the text lists specific extreme hardware specifications (e.g., TPUv3 Pod, NVIDIA A100), massive parameter counts (e.g., 175 billion), or names multiple closed-source competitor models (e.g., GPT-4, Claude Instant). Do not judge the validity of the comparison, only the literal presence of these names and extreme numbers.
proposals.rationale: Well-resourced industry labs often have access to proprietary APIs or massive compute, and their abstracts name-drop these models. This is an upstream factor not inherently tied to conceptual research quality, leaving a strong fingerprint. Seen in R02, R41, and R42.

proposals.name: Residual formatting and markup artifacts
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the raw text contains explicit LaTeX commands (e.g., \textit, \url{}), math environments ($...$), or markdown symbols (**, __) rather than plain text. Do not judge the readability, only the presence of raw markup artifacts.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts scraped with uncompiled LaTeX or markdown tags reveal the author's specific tooling pipeline. A human judge easily ignores these, but they can confuse end-to-end text models. Visible in R09, R23, and R41.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's latex or markdown editing tooling

proposals.name: Rhetorical questions in opening
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the abstract begins with or prominently features direct questions to the reader (e.g., 'Can artificial agents learn...'). Do not judge the effectiveness of the question, only its presence as a stylistic choice.
proposals.rationale: Opening with a rhetorical question is a stylistic fingerprint of non-traditional academic backgrounds or grant-writing practices. It is not a measure of research quality but heavily influences human scoring rubrics. Seen in R06, R07, and R38.

proposals.name: Explicit enumerations and bulleted lists
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the abstract uses explicit bullet points (e.g., •, -) or numbered lists (e.g., (1), 1)) to break up text. Do not judge if the list is well-organized, only if it is formatted as a rigid enumeration rather than standard paragraphs.
proposals.rationale: Standard conference abstracts are usually continuous paragraphs. The use of bulleted lists signals a report or slide-deck writing habit, which a rigid criteria model might reward for clarity while a text model sees it as disjointed text. Seen in R17, R23, and R24.

proposals.name: Use of grandiose adjectives
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the abstract uses superlative or hyperbolic adjectives (e.g., 'remarkable', 'extraordinary', 'strikingly', 'unprecedented') to describe its own results or models. Do not judge the actual impressiveness of the work, only the presence of grandiose descriptors.
proposals.rationale: The use of hype words stems from an upstream culture of marketing research. While it can correlate with genuinely strong results, it is often a superficial feature that inflates rigid criteria judgments without adding mathematical substance. Seen in R02, R37, and R42.

proposals.name: Generic textbook definition openings
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the abstract opens with a broad, dictionary-like definition of the task or field (e.g., 'X is a central problem in Y') rather than jumping straight into the specific novelty. Do not judge the clarity of the writing, only the presence of generic, early-draft definitional boilerplate.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts that read like an early, obvious reading of a prompt or a late-arriving boilerplate often pad the text with obvious dictionary definitions instead of assuming expert knowledge. This positional artifact in the entry stream is not a measure of underlying quality. Seen in R04, R21, and R49.

proposals.name: Explicit repository and link mentions
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the text includes explicit URLs or states that code, checkpoints, or datasets are public (e.g., 'available at github.com/...'). Do not judge the actual reproducibility or code quality, only the explicit textual mention of links or repositories.
proposals.rationale: The presence of links is a fingerprint of institutional rules requiring open-sourcing. Feature-matching models often award points for this explicit keyword matching, whereas an end-to-end model evaluates the text's intrinsic claims, skewing disagreement. Seen in R01, R31, and R47.

proposals.name: Temporal trend-chasing language
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the opening sentences explicitly use temporal markers like 'recently', 'recent surge', or 'until very recently' to frame the problem as a hot trend. Do not judge the trendiness, only the presence of temporal trend-setting words.
proposals.rationale: Texts that emphasize how 'recent' a topic is signal an author jumping on a fast-moving bandwagon. This upstream submission timing is a nuisance variable that rubrics may reward if the trend matches their keywords. Seen in R09, R29, and R42.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing within a hype cycle

proposals.name: Explicit multi-point contribution statements
proposals.instruction: Extent to which the text rigidly enumerates its contributions (e.g., 'This paper makes two main contributions: (1)... (2)...' or 'we provide a novel architecture...'). Do not judge the value of the contributions, only the extent to which they are formatted as an explicit list.
proposals.rationale: Formulaic templates often instruct authors to explicitly list contributions. A rubric easily matches this rigid structure to its 'lists clear contributions' criterion, while an end-to-end model evaluates the underlying conceptual merit regardless of formatting. Seen in R14, R24, and R30.
